messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was forty-nine when his younger brother Stefan died. The call came on a Tuesday afternoon in March—Stefan had been found unresponsive in his apartment in Portland, an overdose, the police said, though the toxicology would take weeks. Marcus had been at his studio in Manhattan when his mother phoned, her voice already fractured. He remembered the exact moment: standing in front of a mood board of Italian fabrics, swatches of charcoal and cream pinned to the wall, and then the world tilting sideways as his mother spoke words that didn't seem to belong in language.

Stefan had been forty-three. He had struggled with addiction for years—a fact that lived in the background of family conversations, acknowledged but somehow never quite real until it was. Marcus had tried to help, had paid for treatment twice, had offered Stefan money and shelter and the kind of practical support that felt like it should matter. But Stefan had always drifted back. In the months before his death, Marcus had begun to distance himself, telling himself it was better to have boundaries, better not to enable. He had stopped calling as frequently. When Stefan reached out, Marcus sometimes didn't respond right away. These were the facts that, when Marcus allowed himself to remember them at all, filled him with a shame so acute it felt like a physical weight.

The funeral was in late April. Marcus sat in the pew next to his wife, Catherine, and felt nothing—or rather, felt everything so intensely that it registered as numbness. He could see his mother's shoulders shaking. He could see the casket. He could see Stefan's friends from high school sitting in the back, people Marcus hadn't thought about in decades. But the moments had a strange, fractured quality. Later, Catherine would tell him what he had said during the reception, and he would have no memory of saying it. There were gaps—whole stretches of time that simply weren't there.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus threw himself into work with a ferocity that surprised even his colleagues. He arrived at the studio before dawn and left after dark. He took on additional projects, volunteered for client presentations he normally would have delegated, kept his mind moving constantly so that it couldn't settle. Catherine mentioned it once—gently, the way she did things—and he had snapped at her, something he rarely did. The studio became the only place that made sense. At home, in the quiet of the evening, the thoughts came: memories of Stefan as a boy, of conversations they'd had, of the times Marcus hadn't answered the phone. The guilt would rise in his chest like something trying to claw its way out, and he would find himself unable to breathe, his heart racing in a way that felt dangerous.

Sleep became impossible. He would lie in bed next to Catherine, his body rigid, his mind cycling through the same terrible loop. He tried to suppress the thoughts, to push them away, but they had a momentum of their own. The only relief came from distraction—he began staying up late, scrolling through his phone, turning on the television, anything to keep his mind occupied. By June, he was functioning on four hours of fragmented sleep most nights.

Catherine noticed that he had stopped planning anything. When she mentioned taking a trip in the fall, or talked about renovating the kitchen, Marcus felt a surge of panic. How could he make plans? How could he think about a future when Stefan didn't have one? The thought felt like a betrayal. He would change the subject abruptly, or tell Catherine they could discuss it later, and later never came.

By August, Catherine's frustration had begun to show. She loved him, she said, but he was disappearing. She didn't recognize him anymore. Marcus knew she was right, but he couldn't seem to stop. When he tried to explain—tried to tell her about the guilt, about the way his body would suddenly flood with terror and shame when something reminded him of Stefan, about the gaps in his memory of the funeral that terrified him—the words came out wrong. He sounded defensive. He sounded like he was blaming her for not understanding.

It was Catherine, finally, who insisted he see someone. She made the appointment herself and told him the date and time. Marcus sat in the therapist's office on a gray September morning, his leg bouncing, his hands clenched, and admitted that he couldn't go on like this. He was afraid of what would happen if he stopped moving, stopped distracting himself, stopped trying not to think. He was afraid that if he allowed himself to fully remember that day, to feel what he had been trying so hard to suppress, he would break entirely. And underneath all of that was something deeper: the certainty that he had failed his brother, that his distance, his boundaries, his refusal to keep rescuing Stefan had somehow contributed to his death. He didn't know how to live with that knowledge, and he didn't know how to live without trying to escape it.
